title: Universal Screening & Toxicology Testing (Minn. Stat. § 260E.32)
sponsor: Pregnancy Health and Substance Use Workgroup
description:
Repeals the current toxicology-testing mandate in section 260E.32 and replaces it with a universal prenatal and birth screening requirement, moved out of the child protection chapter (260E) and reframed as a health-reporting statute.

Under current law, a physician must administer a toxicology test to a pregnant patient (or a newborn) whenever obstetrical complications suggest possible nonmedical drug use, and a positive result is reported as a neglect referral under 260E.31/260E.03. Testing is therefore targeted, complication-triggered, and wired directly into the child protection reporting pipeline.

**Why it matters:** Tying a medical test directly to a child protection report creates a strong disincentive for pregnant people to disclose substance use or seek prenatal care in the first place — a patient who suspects a positive test could trigger a CPS referral has a reason to avoid care altogether. This proposal breaks that link:

- Replaces targeted, complication-triggered toxicology testing with universal screening (a verbal or written validated tool) for every pregnant or birthing person, with referrals to services based on need rather than a positive drug test
- Makes toxicology testing itself optional and clinical — administered only when it serves a medical purpose in treating the patient or infant, not as a reporting trigger
- Redirects toxicology test reporting to the Department of Health as public health data (protected under section 13.384) instead of automatically routing it through child protection
- Requires confirmatory testing from an accredited laboratory before a positive result can be reported, reducing false positives feeding into the system
- Preserves the existing mandated-reporter duty to report prenatal substance exposure separately, under 260E.03/260E.06/260E.31 — this section stops being the mechanism that does that reporting itself

title: Narrowing the Definition of Prenatal-Exposure Neglect (Minn. Stat. § 260E.03)
sponsor: Pregnancy Health and Substance Use Workgroup
description:
Narrows the statutory definition of "neglect" so that prenatal exposure to alcohol or a controlled substance is only maltreatment if it demonstrably harms the infant — not simply because a test came back positive.

Current law (260E.03, subd. 15(5)) defines prenatal substance exposure itself as neglect, evidenced by withdrawal symptoms, a positive toxicology test, developmental delays, or a fetal alcohol spectrum disorder diagnosis — with no separate requirement that the exposure actually caused harm.

**Why it matters:** Under the current standard, exposure and harm are treated as the same thing, which is the core problem this proposal (together with the 260E.32 rewrite) is designed to fix.

- Rewrites clause (5) so a report of prenatal exposure to alcohol or a controlled substance only counts as neglect when it "adversely affects the infant's health, basic needs, and safety" — exposure alone is no longer sufficient
- Broadens the substance covered from "controlled substance" to "alcohol or a controlled substance" explicitly, and updates the cross-referenced definition from section 253B.02 to section 152.02
- Separately loosens clause (7), the general caregiver substance-misuse standard, from requiring "chronic and severe" use to "chronic or severe" use — lowering the bar for that unrelated category even as clause (5) raises it for prenatal exposure specifically
- Sets up the two-track reporting structure created in the companion changes to 260E.31: harmful exposure becomes a maltreatment report, exposure without demonstrated harm becomes a non-maltreatment safe-care notification

title: Reporting & Response to Prenatal Substance Exposure (Minn. Stat. § 260E.31)
sponsor: Pregnancy Health and Substance Use Workgroup
description:
Rewrites the reporting and response framework for prenatal substance exposure in 260E.31 — replacing a single, CPS-only reporting pipeline with a two-track system, and repealing the mandate that local welfare agencies pursue emergency civil commitment against a pregnant person who declines services.

**Why it matters:** This is the operational heart of the package. Three changes matter most:

- **Removes the mandatory civil commitment trigger.** Current law requires the local welfare agency to seek an emergency admission under section 253B.051 if a pregnant person refuses recommended voluntary services or fails treatment. This proposal deletes that mandate outright, replacing compelled commitment with a voluntary, services-based response — removing what has been one of the most coercive features of current law and a significant deterrent to disclosure.
- **Splits post-birth handling into two tracks.** A "Reports at birth" track continues into the standard child maltreatment process, but only where exposure adversely affects the infant's basic needs and safety (mirroring the narrowed 260E.03 definition). A new "Notification at birth" track routes exposure without demonstrated harm to a state CAPTA portal instead — explicitly not a maltreatment report — aligning Minnesota with the federal Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act's Plan of Safe Care notification requirement.
- **Reframes the response to reports made during pregnancy** around a "plan of safe care" — coordinated services (prenatal care, substance use treatment, mental health services, housing, transportation, etc.) for the infant and family — replacing the narrower "offer services indicated under the circumstances" standard, and broadens the mandatory-reporting exemption so a professional coordinating any recommended health care for the patient (not just prenatal care specifically) can avoid triggering a report while treatment continues.

Language throughout the section is also updated from "woman" to "pregnant person," and cross-references are updated to match the revised definitions in 260E.03 and 260E.32.

title: Plug-In Solar Photovoltaic Devices (Minn. Stat. § 216B.2429)
sponsor: Rep. Larry Kraft (DFL-St. Louis Park), with 21 co-authors
description:
Creates a new statute, Minn. Stat. § 216B.2429, establishing a lightweight regulatory category for small, portable "plug-in" solar devices — often called balcony or deck-mounted solar — and exempting qualifying devices from the interconnection-agreement and net metering rules that otherwise apply to anything connected to a customer's home electrical system.

Under current law, any device tied into a customer's electrical system, regardless of size, falls under the same interconnection agreement and net metering framework built for permanent, professionally installed rooftop solar arrays. That process can involve utility approval, inspection, and paperwork that takes weeks — workable for a homeowner installing a full rooftop system, but impractical for a renter or condo resident who wants to plug a small panel into a wall outlet to offset household electricity use. These devices are common in Europe but have had no clear legal pathway in Minnesota.

**Why it matters:** This proposal creates that pathway by treating small, certified plug-in solar devices as categorically different from grid-tied installations, rather than forcing them through a regulatory process designed for a different scale of equipment:

- Defines a "plug-in solar photovoltaic device" as a portable photovoltaic device that primarily offsets a portion of a customer's electricity consumption, has a maximum power output of 1,200 watts, can connect to an on-site energy storage system, and is listed or certified as compliant with interactive plug-in photovoltaic equipment standards by a testing laboratory recognized under OSHA's Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory program
- Exempts qualifying devices from having to enter an interconnection agreement with an electric utility
- Exempts qualifying devices from Minnesota's net metering provisions under section 216B.164
- Bars electric utilities from imposing any fee, condition, approval, or reporting requirement on a qualifying device's installation or operation
- Shields electric utilities from liability for damage or injury caused by a plug-in solar photovoltaic device
- Is aimed at renters and multifamily-building residents, who typically cannot install traditional rooftop solar because they don't own or control the building's electrical infrastructure

Introduced February 23, 2026, with Rep. Larry Kraft as lead author and 21 co-authors; referred to the House Energy Finance and Policy Committee, with authors continuing to be added through April 22, 2026.
